verses.150:1: Louvai o Senhor {sanctis}: * louvai-o {firmamento} do seu poder.
verses.150:2: Louvai-o {virtutibus}: * louvai-o segundo a multidão da sua grandeza.
verses.150:3: Louvai-o {sono} da trombeta: * louvai-o com o saltério e a cítara.
verses.150:4: Louvai-o com o {tympano} e {choro}: * louvai-o com as cordas e {organo}.
verses.150:5: Louvai-o com címbalos {benesonantibus}: † louvai-o com címbalos {jubilationis}: * {spiritus} louve o Senhor.

decisions.why: The Latin form can be masculine ('among his saints') or neuter ('in his holy places'). The Greek ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις αὐτοῦ is just as open. DRB chose 'holy places'. MS1932 has 'santuário', which is the Hebrew's singular. Portuguese cannot keep both readings, since 'santos' can only be persons. My ruling copies 67:36, where the same Latin and the same Greek (*Mirábilis Deus in sanctis suis*) already read 'nos seus santos' in this psalter (rule 6). The line then runs straight into 150:2, which has 'nos seus poderes'. The cost is the place-reading. The glossary row *sancta* (a place) → 'o lugar santo' (D10) is for *sancta* where it clearly means a place (133:2), and it stays an option here.

options.label: nos seus santos
options.note: Ruling. Same wording as 67:36 for the same Latin and the same Greek.

options.label: no seu lugar santo
options.note: The place-reading, singular as D10 rules for *sancta*.

options.label: nos seus lugares santos
options.note: DRB 'holy places'. The plural is heard as the Holy Land sites (D10).

options.label: no seu santuário
options.note: MS1932, DM1962, CNBB. This is the Hebrew's singular, and *sanctuárium* has its own word.

decisions.why: D31 splits *firmaméntum* into 'esteio' (God as a support) and 'firmamento' (the sky), and it names 150:1 as a place for this psalm to decide. Here the vault is a place where praise is given. It pairs with 'in sanctis', and DRB and MS1932 both have 'firmament'. So the sky-word stands. The genitive 'virtútis ejus' → 'do seu poder' follows the *virtus* row. The one other reading is 'the firm hold of his power' (στερέωμα, 'solidity'), which is the 72:4 row's 'firmeza'. It is kept as an option.

options.label: no firmamento
options.note: Ruling. D31, the sky. MS1932 has the same words.

options.label: na firmeza
options.note: The 'solidity' sense, as at 72:4.

decisions.why: The plural *virtútes* is 'os seus poderes' at 77:4b, 102:21 and 148:2 (in 148:2 these are the heavenly powers, beside the angels). DRB 'for his mighty acts' and MS1932 'por seus prodígios' both read *in* as 'for'. The Latin's *in* keeps the same shape as *in sanctis* in the verse before. Keeping 'nos' leaves the Latin's reading open: in his mighty works, or among his powers, the hosts of 148:2. 'pelos' would close it.

options.label: nos seus poderes
options.note: Ruling. The Latin's *in* is kept, and so is the echo with 150:1.

options.label: pelos seus poderes
options.note: DRB 'for'. This decides that the powers are the cause of praise.

options.label: pelos seus prodígios
options.note: MS1932. *prodígium* is another Latin word.

decisions.why: *tuba* → 'trombeta' (46:6, 80:4, 97:5). *sonus* → 'som' (18:5, 41:5b). *in* + a sound → 'ao', following 46:6 *in voce tubæ* → 'à voz da trombeta'. This is the Portuguese idiom 'ao som de', and MS1932 and DM1962 print the same words. The rest of the psalm has 'com', because there the *in* goes with an instrument, not a sound.

options.label: ao som
options.note: Ruling. Same wording as 46:6 'à voz da trombeta'. MS1932.

options.label: com o som
options.note: Keeps the same preposition through all ten imperatives.

decisions.why: The glossary row *týmpanum* → 'tamborim' (67:26, 80:3) names 150:4 among its places. The DRB word 'timbrel' is a hand-drum with jingles, which is the tamborim. 149:3 (in progress in parallel) has the same noun.

options.label: tamborim
options.note: Ruling. The glossary row.

options.label: tambor
options.note: The CNBB LH wording.

options.label: timbale
options.note: MS1932. In Brazil a timbale is an orchestral kettledrum.

decisions.why: Latin *chorus* (Greek χορός, the same word in both places) is first 'a dance in a ring, a choral dance'. After that it is the band that dances and sings, and then a choir (L&S). My first pencil was 'a dança': the dance is the first sense, and the word stands beside the drum. But Ps 149:3 *in choro* (ἐν χορῷ), drafted in parallel and read by its three readers with no remark on the word, ruled for the cognate: 'Louvem o seu nome em coro'. The two psalms are sung one after the other at Lauds, so rule 6 wants one word. Here *chorus* is joined to *týmpano* under one *in*, so the noun stays a noun: 'com o tamborim e o coro'. That is 149's word in 150's syntax. MS1932's 'e em coro' would make it an adverb, and 149's 'no coro' sense (the choir-stalls) was already refused there. The cost: 'coro' is heard as a body of singers, and the dance that the Latin's first sense and the Greek carry is not heard. 'a dança' is the CNBB's wording too, which proves only that the line is known in Brazil. If either psalm moves to the dance, both should move together.

options.label: o coro
options.note: Ruling. The cognate, as in 149:3 'em coro' and DRB 'choir'. The noun is kept as a noun beside the drum.

options.label: em coro
options.note: Exactly 149:3's words and MS1932's ('com timbales e em coro'). Adverbial: 'in chorus, together'.

options.label: a dança
options.note: L&S sense I, and the Greek χορός. Heard as dance only, without the song. The CNBB has the same word.

decisions.why: The glossary row *órganum* → 'instrumento' (136:2 'os nossos instrumentos'; ὄργανον in both places). Portuguese 'órgão', as in DRB 'organs' and MS1932 'órgão', is heard first as the church pipe organ, an instrument the psalm does not mean. L&S gives *órganum* in the Vulgate as 'a pipe' (citing Gen 4:21), and 'flauta' is also the CNBB's wording from the Hebrew *ugab*. I keep the precedent. 'instrumento' is exactly what the word *órganum* says, it leaves open what the Latin leaves open, and it keeps one Greek word as one Portuguese word (D15's test). The cost: in a list of named instruments it sounds generic. 'a flauta' is the strongest option.

options.label: o instrumento
options.note: Ruling. Same as 136:2 and the glossary row.

options.label: a flauta
options.note: The Vulgate sense in L&S, 'a pipe'. It names one instrument.

options.label: o órgão
options.note: The cognate, as in DRB and MS1932. Heard as the church pipe organ.

decisions.why: *benesonans* means 'sounding well' (εὐήχοις). 'sonoro' in Portuguese means both loud and full-toned, pleasant to hear ('voz sonora'), so one ordinary adjective carries the compound. MS1932, DM1962 and the CNBB LH all say 'címbalos sonoros', so the phrase is already known in Brazil. 'bem sonantes' is a calque and sounds bookish. 'melodiosos' adds melody. 'címbalos' has no article, as in the Latin and MS1932.

options.label: sonoros
options.note: Ruling. MS1932, DM1962, CNBB.

options.label: de bom som
options.note: Both halves of the compound, spelled out.

options.label: bem sonantes
options.note: The calque.

decisions.why: D43 settles the *jubiláre / jubilátio* family as 'aclamar / aclamação' (ἀλαλαγμός, the war-shout and cheer). That row names 150:5 among its places. The Greek here is ἀλαλαγμοῦ, as at 46:6. MS1932 and the CNBB have 'de júbilo', which the glossary keeps for *gáudium*. Its cost is that 'címbalos de aclamação' is less familiar than 'címbalos de júbilo'.

options.label: de aclamação
options.note: Ruling. D43.

options.label: de júbilo
options.note: MS1932, CNBB. Collides with *gáudium*'s word.

decisions.why: This is the last line of the Psalter. The Greek is πνοή ('breath'), not πνεῦμα. The Latin chose *spíritus*, which holds both breath and spirit, and DRB keeps it ('let every spirit'). Everywhere else in this psalter *spíritus* of a living being is 'espírito' (31:2, 103:29–30, 145:4). 'sopro' is for 102:16, where wind and breath are one image. 'tudo o que respira' (MS1932; also every Hebrew-based version, e.g. ARA 'todo ser que respira', see circulation.md) is an explanation. It turns the noun into a clause and closes the word to 'breathing beings'. 'todo espírito' has no article, so it is 'every spirit', not 'the whole spirit'. It is heard as souls, angels and every spirit. That is the Latin's own word, and a reader crossing columns finds it. The known Brazilian line is lost, and it comes from the Hebrew.

options.label: todo espírito
options.note: Ruling. The Latin's word, as in DRB 'every spirit'.

options.label: todo sopro
options.note: The breath-sense (πνοή). As the 102:16 row.

options.label: tudo o que respira
options.note: MS1932. Paraphrase. Known in Brazil in Hebrew-based versions.

choices.150:1: No title. DO's Psalm150.txt opens at 'Laudáte Dóminum in sanctis ejus'. It has no 'Allelúja' line, although the LXX and MS1932 have one. As in Pss 146–147, nothing is added (D7). *laudáte* → 'louvai' with a direct object, and *laudáte eum* → 'louvai-o', as 116:1 and 148:1–2. The tenfold imperative is kept word for word (rule 6: repetitions stay).
choices.150:2: *secúndum multitúdinem magnitúdinis ejus* → 'segundo a multidão da sua grandeza'. These are the *multitúdo* row (which notes that 150:2 has both nouns) and *magnitúdo* → 'grandeza' (70:8, 78:11, 144:3, 144:6). MS1932 has the same words.
choices.150:3: *psaltérium* → 'saltério' and *cíthara* → 'cítara' (glossary rows; 56:9 = 107:3 'saltério e cítara', in the Latin's order). One 'com' serves both nouns, as the Latin has one *in* (97:5). The colon ends on the proparoxytone 'cítara' where the Latin ends on 'cíthara' (as 91:4, 146:7).
choices.150:4: *chordæ* → 'as cordas' (DRB 'strings'). MS1932's 'instrumentos de corda' explains the word. One 'com' serves each pair, as the Latin has one *in*.
choices.150:5: The Latin's '(6)' marker is not reproduced (rule 4). The verse keeps its † and *. The last colon is a jussive subjunctive ('louve'), like *laudet*. This verse, with the whole psalm, is also said in the priest's thanksgiving after Mass (DO missa/Latin/Ordo/Post.txt) and at Lauds of Holy Saturday (missa/Latin/Tempora/Quad6-6r.txt), found by grep.

audit.note: Drafted at psalm level from the parallels (consult/parallels/ps150.md), with lookups in the finished psalms (ps150/concord.py, copied from ps149's) and the glossary rows for every instrument. Brazilian circulation was fetched (circulation.md): the CNBB LH text is from the Hebrew, and none of it is taken. Precedent followed: 46:6 (à voz da trombeta → ao som da trombeta), 56:9/107:3 (saltério e cítara), 67:26/80:3 (tamborim), 136:2 (órganum → instrumento), 67:36 (in sanctis suis → nos seus santos), 148:2 (virtútes → poderes), D31 (firmamento, the sky), D43 (jubilátio → aclamação). Hard readings: 150:1 *in sanctis* (persons or places), 150:4 *chorus* (dance, not choir) and *órganum* (instrument, not organ), 150:5 *omnis spíritus*. 150:4 *chorus* was first pencilled 'a dança'. Before the readers it was aligned with Ps 149:3 ('em coro', ruled in parallel and read without remark) as 'o coro'; see decision `choro`.

Hard checks pass. Every length flag is short, not long: 150:1b −3, 150:2 −4/−4, 150:5a −5, 150:5b −3. They come mostly from the refrain. *Laudáte eum* has five syllables and 'louvai-o' has three, and that comes twice in every verse. 150:5a also loses syllables because *benesonántibus* (six) becomes 'sonoros' (three). All of them are accepted, since a shorter colon still fits one breath. Every mediant and final ends on a paroxytone or oxytone except 150:3b 'cítara', which falls exactly where the Latin has 'cíthara'.
